5.90.m: Devaśarman said: / The sin committed in my previous birth has indeed been recounted by you as mine: / in the state of a Śūdra, O foremost of Brahmins, wealth was thus amassed by me.
How then was the status of a Brahmin attained by me, O best of the twice-born? / Tell me the entire cause of that, O scholar learned in theoretical and experiential wisdom!
Birth in the realm of Bhārata is rare, and human existence is rarer still from that; / among human lives, Brahminhood is exceedingly difficult to attain, especially arising from a good lineage.
Even there, such a wife—all-knowing, speaking sweetly, / virtuous, and endowed with all good qualities—how did such a rare one come to be?
Vasiṣṭha said: / Whatever deed you undertook previously, the righteous action performed, O twice-born, / that I shall declare; let it be heard if you think fit.
There was a certain righteous Brahmin, of virtuous conduct and highly learned, / a devotee of Viṣṇu, truly righteous in nature, constantly devoted to Viṣṇu.
Simply for the sake of bathing in sacred waters, he wandered the earth alone; / while roaming, that noble-minded one arrived at your house.
At the mere sight of him, good sense arose in you, / for the arrival of the virtuous takes place only in a house that has turned toward righteousness.
What, indeed, is not obtained, O Brahmin, by serving a Brahmin Vaiṣṇava? / Even that which is hard to obtain in the world, the permanent abode of liberation, [is attained].
A single place was requested by him merely for lodging, O best of men; / it was given by your wife alone, and by you along with your sons.
"Come, come comfortably into my house, O Brahmin!" / Thus you said repeatedly to the holy Vaiṣṇava Brahmin:
"May you dwell here comfortably; this house is yours, O you of noble vows! / Today I am blessed, today I am holy, today I have visited a sacred place!
Today the fruit of a pilgrimage has been obtained by me through the sight of you, O Brahmin!" / A dwelling place, the supreme sacred shelter of cows, was shown to him.
A massage of his limbs was thoroughly performed, and his feet were rubbed; / they were washed with water, and you bathed in the water from his feet.
Freshly made ghee, curds, milk, and various other offerings were presented / to that Brahmin at that time by you, impelled by good fortune.
Thus that Brahmin was gratified by you along with your wife / and together with your sons—that highly fortunate Vaiṣṇava, learned in wisdom.
Then, at a clear dawn in the month of Mādhava, / while setting out for the Gaṅgā to bathe, he, delighted with compassion,
taught before you the glorification of bathing in Vaiśākha; / and he had you perform it properly along with your wife and son.
Just as there is no body of water in the world equal to the ocean, / even so there is no month like Vaiśākha, which is dear to Mādhava.
Sins remain without obstacle in the body / only so long as this month of Mādhava, the destroyer of impurities, does not arrive.
Having heard his words, service was performed in Vaiśākha; / with a contented mind, O Brahmin, Madhusūdana was worshipped.
Only five days remained of that month; / beginning from the eleventh day, the bath was performed in accordance with the rules.
Through association with that Brahmin, and daily at the Revā, / the morning bath was performed by you, O Brahmin, for that much time in the month of Vaiśākha.
The Lord of the gods, the slayer of Madhu, the supreme Lord, was worshipped; / the entire month had not been obtained by you previously for the purpose of bathing.
In this way the bath was observed by you, though consisting of only five days; / by that merit, and especially through company with the Brahmin,
and by the grace of Govinda, you attained Brahminhood; / through the connection with that month, this great lineage was obtained by you,
which is difficult to obtain among the gods of the earth, endowed with truth and righteousness; / also a truly chaste wife was attained, virtuous and endowed with all good qualities,
born in the house of Cyavana, all-knowing and a proclaimer of the Veda. / Beauty alone is the foremost ornament of women, O great sage;
good conduct is the second, and truthfulness is the third; / constant nobility is the fourth, and excellent merit is the fifth;
sweetness is the sixth, and great purity is the seventh— / outward and inward, constantly the seventh ornament of all ornaments for women;
devotion to the husband is the eighth, service is the ninth indeed, / forbearance is the tenth, and delight is the eleventh;
fidelity to the husband is remembered as the twelfth for women, O foremost of Brahmins. / Adorned with these is your virtuous wife, the proclaimer of the Veda.
She was obtained respectfully through the merit connected with bathing in Vaiśākha; / what, indeed, that is extremely difficult to attain is not obtained in the month of Mādhava
through bathing and through worshipping the supreme Lord according to the rules? / However, you were bewildered by delusion, and your mind was pervaded by craving.
In your previous birth, O Brahmin, wealth was merely hoarded; / it was not given to Brahmins, nor to the poor, nor to others by you.
Not to your kinsmen, nor to your sons and wife was it given in any way; / while dying, greed alone was contemplated by you.
Nothing was given, no oblation offered, no mantra chanted, nor was death met in a sacred place; / nor indeed was the god Nārāyaṇa meditated upon, who destroys all sins.
When wealth is available, a man becomes a miser; / he who dies without giving—what indeed is more sorrowful than that?
Birth in an [illustrious] family is obtained only by austerity, bathing at sacred places, and the like; / without giving, O Brahmin, nothing at all attends [a man in the next life].
Due to the effect of that sin, poverty came upon you; / you became childless, constantly afflicted with sorrow.
From the glorification of bathing in Vaiśākha, even though lasting only five days, / from the worship of Hari at that time, and from association with the Brahmin,
birth was obtained in a [noble] family, O Brahmin, and Brahminhood, which is hard to obtain; / and a good son, a Brahmin lineage, wealth, grain, excellent wives,
a good birth and an auspicious death, excellent enjoyment and happiness, / an intellect always inclined toward giving, generosity, and supreme fortitude [were granted].
By the grace of that god Viṣṇu, the great-souled / Nārāyaṇa, the desired accomplishments arise, O Brahmin.
In the month of Ūrja, in the month of Tapas, and in Mādhava, which is dear to Mādhava, / having bathed and [honored] Dāmodara, Mādhava, and Madhusūdana with devotion,
having specially worshipped [them] and given gifts with devotion, / having attained earthly happiness, a person then goes to Hari.
The multitude of sins accumulated across many births dissolves through bathing in Mādhava, / just as darkness vanishes at sunrise, O Brahmin; the self-born Brahmā himself declared this word.
Viṣṇu made a pure deliberation, and first established the single observance of the month of Mādhava, / having contemplated in his mind the secret of Yama, so that human beings might go to heaven.
Therefore, when this month of Mādhava, beloved of Mādhava, has arrived, / having bathed in sacred water at a pilgrimage place now before sunrise,
and having worshipped Mukunda, Madhusūdana, according to the prescribed rule, / [you will obtain] sons, grandsons, wealth, auspiciousness, and desired pleasures;
having enjoyed [them], you will then attain imperishable heaven at your death. / Everything that was undertaken and done by you in your previous birth,
that deed has been recounted by me before you, O Brahmin. / Knowing this, O highly fortunate one, especially in the month of Vaiśākha,
having bathed properly according to rule, worship Madhusūdana. / Having worshipped the divine Govinda, the flawless Nārāyaṇa,
you will attain happiness, a son, wealth, and the imperishable Hari.

Nārada said:
Enlightened indeed by the son of Brahmā, that best of brāhmaṇas, full of noble majesty / and filled with joy, bowed down there with devotion to Vasiṣṭha.
Taking leave of the brāhmaṇa, he went home. The great sage said to his wife Sumanā: / 'Indeed, the entire account of my past deeds has been revealed by that very brāhmaṇa, through your favor,
O auspicious one, by Vasiṣṭha; this very day my delusion has been dispelled. / I shall propitiate Madhusūdana with devotion, having bathed in the glorious month of Mādhava.'

Nārada said:
Hearing his supreme, purifying, deeply auspicious speech, which brought about great good fortune, / she, filled with joy, said to her husband: 'Blessed are you, having been awakened by the brāhmaṇa.'

5.91.m:
Nārada said:
The highly wise Devaśarman, together with that Sumanā, / at the sacred, celebrated pilgrimage site of Kanakhala on the Gaṅgā,
performed his bath according to rule in Vaiśākha, while the sun was in Aries, / and worshipped unswerving Madhusūdana according to rule.
Endowed with moral restraints and religious observances, he then gave whatever he could according to his means, / eating sacrificial food, sleeping on the ground, and abiding by the vow of celibacy.

Emaciated through austerities such as the Kṛcchra penance, meditating on Nārāyaṇa in his heart, / having reached the full-moon day of Vaiśākha there, and having given honey, sesame seeds, and the like,
having fed the brāhmaṇas and given with devotion a cow along with a sacrificial fee, / he prayed to the brāhmaṇas there that his bath might be without defect.
She too, virtuous and beautifully proportioned, dedicated to devotion toward her husband, / constantly served her husband after bathing and worshipping Keśava.
Then that husband and wife went to their own house, deeply delighted, / considering themselves to have accomplished their purpose, without any doubt.
By the power of that religious merit, after a certain time, indeed, / his riches, grains, and prosperities became immeasurable.
There were four sons, endowed with modesty, skilled in Vedic scripture, / knowing dharma, devoted to Viṣṇu, and always dedicated to their father and mother;
they became men of boundless intellect, awakened to the aims of life, / renowned, knowing the reality of ritual injunctions, knowing Brahman, and intent on Brahman;
endowed with every virtue, their fame was established.

That couple, having enjoyed the fruition of merit consisting of abundant bliss accompanied by sons, then after a long time, / reached the highest, supreme abode through devotion to Him, O king, and by the grace of the good deed done in the glorious month of Mādhava.
Just as Mādhava himself is remembered as the direct lord of wisdom and fortune, / even so is the month of Mādhava beloved to Madhusūdana.
This glorification of the month of Mādhava has been told to you in brief, O sinless one, / O hero, by me, just as it was heard long ago from my father.

5.92.m:
Sūta said:
Having heard this speech of Nārada, that king / bowed down, astonished, and spoke, contemplating Hari in his mind.

Ambarīṣa said:
How is this, O sage? We are bewildered that with such slight effort / a śūdra of sinful conduct attained supreme brāhmaṇahood!
Brāhmaṇahood is hard to obtain, dear sir, even through diverse good deeds; / how did that lowest person attain it merely through a bath in the month of Mādhava?
Not by sacrifices, gifts, severe austerities, nor by other acts called meritorious, O lord, / do kings like us, however wealthy, attain the status of earthly gods!

Even that son of Gādhi, having performed diverse, dreadful austerities for a long time, constantly, / attained it with difficulty after a full hundred years, oh, somehow through many strenuous efforts!
How did this lowest of castes, this sinner, destitute of his own dharma, wealthy yet ungenerous, / attain the state of brāhmaṇahood here from that small, effortless merit?

Nārada said:
You have spoken the truth, O king: brāhmaṇahood is exceedingly hard to obtain; / nevertheless, the courses of dharma are subtle and difficult to comprehend in reality.
Diverse are actions, diverse is the creation of living beings, / diverse are beings, and diverse are the potencies of actions.
Sometimes a meritorious action, which was acquired and lay dormant, / is increased, O king, by some auspicious action;
it bestows a very great fruit, even in that very birth. / This dharma is deep and subtle; it cannot be inferred arbitrarily.
No certainty of time is heard regarding that giving of fruit: / whatever meritorious action has been covered by intervening sins,
it suddenly appears from somewhere, at some time, and bestows excellent fruit. / There is no destruction in this world of what has been done, whether merit or sin.
Even so, terrible sin departs through numerous merits. / As for what was said by you, O king, that [the result] must correspond to the magnitude of exertion,
and the fruit depends on that: hear the truth spoken by me on that matter as well. / If smallness and greatness depended upon lack of exertion and great exertion,
then hired laborers and the like would constantly be performing the greatest vows! / Great efforts are involved in collecting the urine of lions, tigers, and the like;
hence [on that reasoning] this would surpass the praise of the five products of the cow among vows! / If greatness lay in the multiplicity of prescribed duties, then smallness
would apply to entering water, fire, and the like, compared to another vow. / Therefore, 'this is small, that is great' is not a governing rule;
the great reward is precisely what is stated in the scripture. / Just as the small is destroyed by the great, so too the great is destroyed by the small;
for is not the destruction of heaps of grass seen by a tiny spark? / Even Ajāmila, O king, remembered as the husband of a maidservant,
abandoning his lawful wife, always dwelling on the path of sin, / called out to his son at the point of death, uttering 'Nārāyaṇa!';
and thus, by uttering His name, he attained an exceedingly rare station. / Just as fire, when touched even involuntarily, burns,
so too does the name Govinda burn away [sins], even when uttered deceitfully or by pretext.
Ten thousand murders, a thousand terrible breaches of vows, cohabitation with crores of teachers' wives, / and countless thefts are instantly destroyed by the name Govinda, beloved of Hari.
Whatever small good deed imbued with devotion to Viṣṇu is done / by a wise and virtuous person, O hero, its fruit becomes inexhaustible.
No doubt should be entertained: having propitiated Mādhava with devotion in the month of Mādhava, / a person will obtain whatever he desires.
Offspring, wealth, wife, land, palace, horses, elephants, / pleasures, heaven, and liberation are not far from devotion to Hari.
Thus, according to the rule prescribed in the scripture, even by a slight [act], without doubt, / there can be the destruction of even great sin through proper procedure.
Superiority of fruit, O wise one, comes from the intensity of inner feeling and ritual action; / subtle are the ways of dharma, hard to understand even for the gods.
This month of Mādhava is dear to the great-souled Mādhava; / it alone is capable of granting every desire in the three worlds.
If a wise donor, though ruined in intention since birth, somehow remains devoted to bathing / in the holy water of the Gaṅgā at the right time and place, he is still not purified—this is my view.

Even if one enters a fire fed with ghee and oil, having flames curling to the right, and is burned at the proper time, / if corrupted in intention, he indeed attains neither heaven nor any other fruit.

Even if gods dwell constantly in sacred places such as the Gaṅgā and in temples, / along with the hosts of yakṣas, they go to destruction if they observe fasts devoid of proper disposition; they obtain no fruit from it.
Therefore, placing his disposition in the heart-lotus, he who, pure and intent on bathing, / worships glorious Mādhava with devotion in the month of Mādhava—we are not able to describe his merit.
In this regard also, listen to an ancient occurrence, O king; / I shall recount a marvelous fruit of deeds.
How, through the grace of that month of Mādhava and of Mādhava himself, / even a certain brāhmaṇa woman, though wanton, obtained an auspicious fruit.
Formerly, the ruler of Kāñcī was famous as Divodāsa. / He had a daughter who was a great gem, always the foremost among women,
endowed with virtues and beauty, well-behaved, charming and auspicious, / famous by the name Divyādevī, incomparable on earth in beauty.
She was gazed upon by her father, endowed with form and charm. / Then Divodāsa, having seen his virtuous daughter Divyādevī,
[thought:] “To what noble, excellent groom shall this maiden be given?” / Becoming filled with concern and looking around, that best of men,

Recognizing fully the king of the Rūpa country, the lord of the earth,
then the king summoned the great-souled Citrasena.
Divodāsa gave the maiden to the wise Citrasena. / When the time of her marriage arrived, O king,
that Citrasena indeed died according to the law of time. / And the righteous king Divodāsa pondered.
And summoning brāhmaṇas, O delight of kings, he asked: / “At the time of her marriage, Citrasena has gone to heaven.
What fate will be hers? Let them tell me.” / The brāhmaṇas said: “O king, the marriage of a maiden occurs according to injunction.
If the husband meets with death, or if he abandons her, / or terrified by a great illness, he abandons her and departs,
or becomes an ascetic, O king, it is seen in the treatises on dharma / that when she has attained puberty, another husband is ordained.
The father may certainly perform the marriage through a representative; there is no doubt. / Thus it is instructed in the treatise on dharma by auspicious people, O king.
Let her marriage be performed!” Thus spoke those best of the twice-born. / And the righteous Divodāsa, impelled by the brāhmaṇas,
set his mind on marriage, O great king. / Divyādevī was given again in marriage, O best of kings,
to the meritorious Puṣpasena, that noble king. / But that king too went to the condition of death at the time of the wedding.
Whenever the fortunate king, her father, / made an effort for the marriage of Divyādevī, very distressed,
at each of those times, when the auspicious moment arrived, the groom also died. / Twenty-one husbands thus died in succession.
Then the king of renowned prowess became very sorrowful. / Consulting with his ministers and remaining resolute, having called him,
the ruler of the earth made up his mind on a svayaṃvara. / Then various kings and rulers were summoned by him
for her svayaṃvara, many who were devoted to dharma. / But perturbed by her beauty, kings sent by death,
the fools waged battle and killed one another. / Thus occurred the destruction of those kṣatriyas, O lord of men.
And Divyādevī, afflicted with grief, then wept piteously. / Seeing that girl weeping and extremely distressed,
the king, having first bowed with a humble neck before the royal priest, / Jātūkarṇa, who knew dharma, was wise, and was an ascetic,
Divodāsa said: / “Tell me, by your favor, what indeed is the sin of this girl, / of my daughter Divyādevī, on account of which this deed was caused?”
Jātūkarṇa said: / “O hero, I shall tell you the conduct of that Divyādevī, / all that was done by her in a previous birth; hear that as I declare it.
There is the sacred city of Vārāṇasī, the destroyer of sin. / In it lived a very wise man named Suvīra,
born in the vaiśya caste, endowed with wealth and grain. / His wife, O very wise one, famous by the name Citrā,
abandoning family conduct, behaved with wicked conduct. / She indeed had no regard for her husband and engaged in terrible deeds.
Devoid of meritorious acts, the evil-minded woman practiced sin. / A wanton woman fond of quarrels, she constantly scolded her husband.
Always dwelling in others' houses, she wandered about excessively. / That wicked woman constantly looked for the faults of others among living beings.
Delighting in slandering the virtuous, that sinful woman always caused much ridicule. / Fond of bad company in her speech, she was dear to wicked people,
cunning, hating righteous people, and speaking untruth. / Knowing this, Suvīra then married another woman.
Together with that new wife, the hero continuously / enjoyed according to his pleasure the sense-objects dear to his heart.
Through righteous conduct, that virtuous soul, always having a mind fixed on truth and merit, / shone, worshipped by his truthful, moderate, virtuous, and well-disposed wife.
Cast out by him, that extraordinary, beautiful Citrā, / then became a wanton woman, averse to association with virtues and dharma.
United with a paramour, she wandered about, having cast off good conduct and lost all shame. / Intent on sinful deeds, she was devoted to the wicked trade of a procuress.
Skilled in the arts of a procuress's craft regarding other women, / she brought about the destruction of households, intent on crookedness of mind.
Calling a virtuous woman, she would incite her with sinful words, / by means of jesting, greed, tales, sport, and causes that produce trust.
That sinful woman would agitate the minds of men and women. / She would deliver noble wives of virtuous men to other men.
She continually practiced deception, devoid of any village of dharma. / Having lived thus for a hundred years, she afterward followed the ways of a prostitute.
Constantly resolved on sin, in time she met with death. / She was born in your house as your daughter named Divyādevī,
beautiful, endowed with form, impelled by her past unseen destiny.” / Nārada said: “Hearing his words, Divodāsa was greatly astonished. / The king spoke sweet words to the sage Jātūkarṇa.”

Divodāsa said: / “If she was of such sinful behavior, having passed away always intent on evil conduct, / how could she become a daughter worthy of me, whose deity is the Lord of Śrī and who am of high lineage?
And how did she obtain a very rare and blessed birth in a vast, prosperous royal family? / By what pure merit, O sage, was she who performed such extraordinary deeds born thus?”
Nārada said: / “Hearing the king's words, the wise sage then / smiled slightly and spoke truthful words.”

Jātūkarṇa said: / “Citrā, deceiving secret lovers and rogues destitute of wealth and intelligence through various sexual encounters, / became a courtesan, having lived measuring out drinks of poison, and in time went to the great, famous city of Nāgapura.
A certain pure-souled brāhmaṇa arrived there in the evening, afflicted with fatigue, / exhausted in that city named Nāga.
Seeing no other place, the bewildered man went to Citrā's house. / He was intensely enchanted by her, the courtesan, through the power of her glance.
With massaging of the feet, a bath, betel, a seat, and food, / and with charming courtesies he was gratified, and he then became free from fatigue.
Then that brāhmaṇa, waited upon by her with varied pleasures of love as if by unseen destiny, / passed the entire night, captivated by the distinction of her devotion.
In the morning, preparing somehow to depart, his heart full of affection, / he, having been pleased with her conduct and her deeds, addressed a word to Citrā with single-minded resolve:
The brāhmaṇa said: / A favor in return must be done by me who am pleased, O beloved! / And I shall tell [you] fully my own deep sorrow.
Listen respectfully to what is auspicious and destroys all sins, / which was spoken of old by brāhmaṇas on the bank of the Narmadā:
He who with diligence bathes even for three days when the sun enters Aries, / before the sun has risen in the month of Mādhava, is freed from masses of sin.
He who performs an outdoor bath during the entire month of Vaiśākha, / and worships god Mādhava according to the rules, is also a destroyer of sins.
Especially at a sacred ford, by means of acts such as bathing and giving gifts / in the month of Mādhava, a human being is freed from great sins.
The heap of great sins remains without hesitation in the body of an embodied being / only as long as he does not gladly bathe at dawn when the lord of day has entered the sign of Aries.
Thus it was heard by me as those brāhmaṇas were speaking, / the supreme boat for crossing the ocean of many sins.
Not far away flows that excellent river Śivadehā; / I will go there to bathe and to destroy my multitude of sins.
If it pleases you, O lovely one, or if your mind has become detached, / then come along with me for the sake of the Vaiśākha bath.
This life is impermanent, and youth is very beautiful; / let it not become for us an irresistible cause for residence in hell.
I was attended by you and cast into the ocean of sin; / for it is true even of great ones that they inhabit evil-abiding bodies.
What is the use of speaking much here? A moment's delay is not proper. / I will deliver you as well, if there is detachment in your heart.
Citrā said: / O master, by the power of destiny, through the virtue of association with you, / my mind has surely become detached toward this reprehensible worldly existence.
Surely this is what I have heard in scripture: association with the virtuous [is supreme]. / Salutations to that inconceivable one, and furthermore to that fixed destiny!
Jātūkarṇa said: / Having spoken thus, Citrā then went with him, / having taken whatever wealth she had, urged on by the sage.
Thereafter that twice-born man, in the month of Vaiśākha, / reached the waters of the Śivadehā and bathed; and the compassionate one then immediately gave [instructions] for her bath.
This kind-hearted brāhmaṇa then caused Citrā, / who spoke charmingly, to bathe according to the proper rite.
There she joyfully heard the glorification of the Vaiśākha bath / while the brāhmaṇas recited the Purāṇas one by one,
by the mere hearing of which the blindness of sin is destroyed, / just as a mass of darkness is destroyed by the very rising of the sun.
Bathed in the auspicious water of the Śivatanū river, she, pure-minded, / by bathing according to the rules, shone spotless like the radiance of the sun.
There, various people desiring infinite worlds bathed in the Revā, / devoted to the service of Hari during Vaiśākha.
Mortals who purify their impure bodies here in the Narmadā that bestows peace, / especially in the month of Mādhava, enjoy the delights of the world of the lords of men.
Remembering the Revā destroys sin from birth; seen, [it destroys sin] born of ten births; / bathed in somehow, [it destroys sin] born of a hundred wombs; served, it grants the world of Rudra.
For the whole month of Mādhava, that Citrā bathed in the water of the Narmadā / and gave gifts according to her ability to the brāhmaṇas daily.
With faith she listened to the hymn to Hari that removes all sins, / recited there by brāhmaṇas, through the association of that twice-born man.
Having bathed in the water of the Revā for the entire month of Mādhava, / Citrā, finding it flawless, also observed the month according to the rite for the earthly gods.
Having built a fresh little hut, that earthly god named Sudeva, / bathing in the water of the Revā, lived there constantly out of compassion due to Citrā's persistence.
Then, in the course of time, the brāhmaṇa met his death; / after him, Citrā also died after a long time, O king.
By that merit of the month of Mādhava, she certainly became your daughter at that very time, / without experiencing the tortures of Yama.
This is the ripening of her action, that she obtained the lineage of a king, / a pure Vaiṣṇava [lineage], O hero, hard to attain by sinful deeds.
The excellent name Divyādevī was given to her, O best of men; / and because she gave food and enjoyable pleasures and comforts
to that brāhmaṇa formerly, even though united with him in courtesanship, / and because she bathed and gave something there in the month of Mādhava,
she enjoys the ripening of the fruit of that gift and that bath: / she drinks cool water and likewise eats sweet food by night.
Enjoying divine pleasures, she lives in the master's house, / and, afflicted with pain, grief, and the like, she eats what destiny gave.
Because formerly she was intent upon destroying the households of men and women, / this slight ripening of her action has come upon her.
By the glorification of the Mādhava bath, without the tortures of Yama, / she, though very sinful, became your beautiful daughter, O hero.
All this conduct of your daughter has been recounted to you, / arising from all her births, O hero, born of good and evil deeds.

5.93.m: Nārada said: / Having thus heard the wondrous speech of Jātūkarṇa, the king, / having bowed to that wise sage, said to him with respect:
Divodāsa said: / How may she now be released from this suffering, O sage? / Jātūkarṇa said: I shall tell of the great merit by which she may become happy.
Though generally kept secret, I shall declare before you / this deed, even though small, [which is] wondrous and destroys hundreds of wrongful acts.
Just as great sin in its entirety comes to destruction by the power of meditating on Hari, / so terrible [sin] meets its dissolution by bathing and giving gifts at dawn in the month of Mādhava.
Just as all serpents perish through fear of Hari, likewise surely / all heaps [of sins] perish when the sun enters Aries and shines, through bathing at a sacred ford and praising Hari.
Like snakes before the splendor of Garuḍa, sins certainly flee / through the bath at dawn in Vaiśākha.
Therefore, O king, Divyādevī should again be given away by yourself, / after hearing [the virtues of] Vaiśākha and listening to the praise that removes sin.
She will be one who shares the pleasure and enjoyment of union with a husband; / and that Sudeva has been born as the mighty ruler of the Pāṇḍya country.
By the merit of the bath in the Revā during the month of Vaiśākha, O king, / give your daughter, purified through bathing, to him alone,
and through hearing the hymn to Mādhava and [worshipping] Mādhava. / No doubt should be entertained in this matter; behold this wonder, O king!
The fruit of her meritorious deed in this world and the next has been fully told. / Nārada said: Having heard this, the king, thus delighted, then [heard] all of it.
He caused his daughter to perform the rite ordained by Jātūkarṇa. / By that very Vīrasena, the ruler of the Pāṇḍya country,
that divine lady was wedded, [he being] her unique friend from a former birth. / Having observed her vows well, she enjoyed abundant worldly pleasures for a long time,
together with Vīrasena, her companion made so by a former birth. / This, O Ambarīṣa, has been told to you in brief,
the glorification of bathing in Vaiśākha. What else do you wish to hear?

5.94.m: Ambarīṣa said: / O Lord, I wish to hear the hymn that quells sins, / by the mere hearing of which a heap of sins melts away.
I am fortunate, I am graced, I have been caused to hear the auspicious rite, / by the very hearing of which that which was accrued through evil deeds falls away.

What wonder is there in this, that in the month of Mādhava whose deity is Madhusūdana, by holy ablutions / and bathings duly performed, a heap of sins should be destroyed, [since] even by reciting His name, a mortal attains His world?

That alone is supreme, pure, and delightful merit, obtainable in this world only through good deeds, / which is spoken of as the name of Keśava; I consider it auspicious in the month of Mādhava, O sage.
Blessed indeed are those who remember the name of Madhusūdana in the month of Mādhava. / Ah, tell me once again some pure deed of His that brings welfare to all beings.
Sūta said: / Hearing the words of that best of kings beloved of Hari, the sage was delighted. / Though eager himself to bathe in the month of Mādhava, he spoke with the relish of the tale of Mādhava.

Nārada said: / It is true, O king: mutual conversation relishing the stories of Mukunda is pure; / along with you, this discourse on the duty of the month of Mādhava dedicated to Hari is even greater than bathing.
He whose life is for dharma, whose dharma is solely for Hari, / and whose days and nights are for merit—him I consider a true Vaiṣṇava on earth.
I shall tell you something, O king, of the fruit born of bathing in Vaiśākha; / even our father [Brahmā] is unable to tell it entirely in detail.
By the mere plunging wherein ghosts have attained liberation / in the month of Mādhava, even sinners [attained it] in the supreme waters of the Narmadā.
Formerly, wandering about on the occasion of [visiting] sacred fords, a certain brāhmaṇa / famed as Muniśarman, righteous, truthful, and pure,
endowed with inner calm and self-control, accompanied by forbearance and contentment, / devoted to ancestral rites, versed in the precepts of Śruti and Smṛti,
devoted to gentle speech, engaged in the worship of Hari, / devoted to the company of Vaiṣṇavas, a sage possessing knowledge of the three times,
intent on his own duties, steadfast, warm-hearted, indifferent to pleasure and displeasure, / compassionate, extremely wise, knower of truth, dear to brāhmaṇas,
walking along in the month of Mādhava to bathe in the Revā, / saw before him five men who were exceedingly miserable,
having no association with one another, dark of body, / having taken shelter under the shade of a banyan tree, sitting and lingering there,
looking in all directions, their minds agitated by sin. / Beholding them, that best of the twice-born was astonished and pondered:
“Who are these men in the forest, terrified, with miserable gestures? / Or are they thieves of disfigured appearance, seen here keeping company,
speaking to one another, emaciated, possessing dark bodies?” / While that foremost brāhmaṇa of steadfast mind was deliberating in this way,
they all approached the sage from a distance with reverence; / folding their hands in supplication and bowing down, they spoke clearly thus.

The five men said: / You are auspicious, the highest of men, shining forth with noble conduct, worthy of honour; / we consider you, O brāhmaṇa, the foremost among the compassionate; hear our word, [and be] friendly to us.
The virtuous are the refuge of the miserable who have become sinners through fate; / the righteous are the removers of suffering of the distressed by their mere sight.
I am a kṣatriya named Vīravāhana from the Pañcāla country. / Out of delusion, I killed a brāhmaṇa with an arrow that pierces by sound.
Bereft of topknot and sacred thread, devoid of forehead-mark, / I wander this earth, declaring: ‘I am a killer of a brāhmaṇa.’
‘Let alms be given to me, a killer of a brāhmaṇa, an extreme sinner!’ / Wandering thus through all sacred fords, I have come here.
Yet the guilt of killing a brāhmaṇa does not leave me even now, O best of sages. / Thus a full year has passed for me acting in this way, O lord,
being burned by sin, my mind confounded by grief. / This other brāhmaṇa who is seen here, O twice-born, is Candraśarman.
He, O brāhmaṇa, is a slayer of his guru, his mind confounded by delusion; / because his mind was confounded by delusion, he is called a slayer of his guru.
Living in the Māgadha country, he was abandoned by his kinsmen on that account; / by fate, O sage, he too has arrived here while wandering.
Bereft of topknot and sacred thread, devoid of brāhmaṇical marks, / when questioned by me about his story, the twice-born spoke only the truth:
that dwelling in the house of his guru, his mind agitated by anger / and overwhelmed by deep delusion, his guru was indeed killed by him.
Consumed by that sin, he lives afflicted by grief. / This third one, O master, is Vedaśarman, [once] self-collected.
A brāhmaṇa, he became a drinker of liquor out of delusion, through associating with a prostitute. / When questioned by me, he also told me what had occurred,
all of his deeds, afflicted as he was by anguish of mind. / Expelled by all people, and even by his wife and relatives,
stained by that sin, he has arrived here while wandering. / This fourth one, named Vidhura, is a vaiśya who violated his guru's bed.
Out of delusion, for three months he enjoyed his mother who had become a prostitute / while staying in the Videha country; then, realizing the truth, wandering about
in misery, he has come to this place, wandering here again, O sage. / This fifth one is a great sinner, one who associates with sinners.
Every day, out of greed for wealth, he committed sins such as theft; / a vaiśya overwhelmed by grave sins, he was thereupon cast out by his own people.
Despondent in mind, he met [us] here by fate, Nanda by name. / In this way, all five most sinful men have reached the same place.
No one makes any contact with anyone through food, clothing, and the like, / O highly fortunate one, except for conversation, O best of the twice-born.
They do not sit on the same seat, nor do they sleep on the same bed. / Thus overwhelmed by grief, we have indeed traveled to various sacred fords,
yet our terrible sin does not depart, O best of sages. / Having seen you shining brightly, our minds have become tranquil.
They say that through the holy sight of a saint like you, sin comes to an end. / Tell us a means, O master, by which the destruction of our sin may come to pass.
You are known by us to be compassionate, O brāhmaṇa, a knower of Vedic meaning, O lord. / For those who are distressed, seeking help, and have come to repentance,
having incurred sins through delusion, you are surely the rescuer. / Nārada said: / Hearing these words of theirs, the sage Muniśarman then,
an ocean of compassion, deliberated thus and spoke: / Muniśarman said: / You have incurred sins through ignorance, yet you speak the truth;
you are filled with remorse; therefore, you are now to be favoured by me. / Hear my true word; raising my arms, I declare [it],
which I heard previously from Aṅgiras at an assembly of sages, / saw in the Vedas and śāstras, and likewise heard from the mouth of my guru.

and by Viṣṇu himself when propitiated of old, it was told in truth:
There is no satisfaction other than eating; there is no guru beyond even a father;

there is no recipient other than brahmins; there is no god higher than Keśava;
there is no holy ford equal to Gaṅgā; there is no gift equal to a milch cow;

there is no prayer equal to the Gāyatrī; there is no vow equal to Dvādaśī;
there is no friend equal to a wife; there is no dawn equal to the rising of dharma;

there is no happiness equal to independence; no stage of life is better than householdership;
there is no conduct higher than truth; there is no happiness higher than contentment;

there is no supreme remover of great sins equal to the month of Mādhava,
when observed according to rule with devotion, beloved of Madhusūdana.

And in holy places like Gaṅgā, it is exceedingly rare;
all penances, beginning with the twelve-year rite,

and sins roar only as long as Mādhava does not arrive.
Whoever, devoted to Hari, bathes for the entire month of Vaiśākha

in water arisen from Hari's foot, pure in mind,
is indeed the slayer of all sins, seen by sinners.
What must be said by the Kinnaras for the expiation of their own heaps of sin?

Whoever bathes in this month known as Mādhava, when [the sun] has entered Aries,
in the sin-warding waters of the Narmadā that bestow happiness, is indeed freed from sins.

For great rivers are hard to attain everywhere in the month of Mādhava;
even harder to attain than that are Gaṅgā, Revā, and Yamunā.

Among these three, having reached even one with respect,
whoever bathes in the month of Mādhava, freed from sin, goes to Hari.

Therefore, alas, together with me in the month of Vaiśākha, the sole essence of merit,
having reached the Revā, may you who have committed sins plunge
into the water of Revā frequented by hosts of sages, for the destruction of the fear of all sins."

Addressed thus, all those sinners, delighted, went with the sage
to the Revā, praising that river of miraculous deeds.

Then Muniśarman, walking along, followed in that way by those men,
saw on the road eight terrifying, frightened Piśācas,

making various noises and wandering here and there,
with upright hair, red eyes raised, black teeth, and emaciated bellies,

in a forest overrun with thorns, devoid of trees and water.
Seeing them running towards him, his mind agitated with fear,
he said: "Homage to Nārāyaṇa! Protect, protect!"

Hearing the name, the sole receptacle of dharma, proclaimed loudly—"Homage to Nārāyaṇa!"—
those Piśācas in their minds attained another existence, obtained by the power of their own destiny.

Observing them with humble minds, Muniśarman,
speaking sweetly, said: "Who are you, disfigured men?

Or what deed was done by whom, through which disfigurement was attained?
Why are all of you like this—miserable and extremely terrifying?"

The ghosts said:
"Constantly afflicted by hunger and thirst, agitated by a multitude of various sorrows,
intent on harshness in our hearts, our consciousness lost, senseless,

we do not know the directions anywhere—fools, killers of human beings.
This that has been told is our misery, and once again, this is our sorrow.

It appears like dawn from the sight of the sunrise,
having heard your gentle speech speaking loudly: 'Nārāyaṇa!'

And having had your sight, O brahmin, we have attained a pure state of being.
By your sight alone, O brahmin, and from hearing Hari's name,

we have attained another existence; we have found compassionate ones.
Sight of a Vaiṣṇava destroys ill-repute, clarifies the intellect,

and generally establishes men [in righteousness].
I am named Paryuṣita; this second one is Sūcaka;

another is Śīghraga; Rodhaka; and this fifth is Lekhaka;
this sixth is Vāgduṣṭa; this seventh is Vidaivata;

and this eighth, a constant beggar, is Kaṣṭadāyaka."
Muniśarman said:
"Whence came the names of you ghosts, born from deeds?

and when ghee was present, [food] devoid of ghee [was given]; therefore, I am Paryuṣita.
Falsely and mendaciously seeking the weak points and secrets of others by nature,

this one denounced [them]; therefore, impure and distressed, he is Sūcaka.
Asked by a hungry brahmin, he fled swiftly;

with this reason in view, O best of the twice-born, he is Śīghraga.
Delicious food was always eaten atop the house by this sinner,

alone, with an evil mind; therefore, he is remembered as Rodhaka.
Remaining always in silence, he writes upon the earth with his foot;

this most sinful one even among us, joined with people, is Lekhaka.
This one hates the virtues of the virtuous and recognizes virtue in the vicious;

and he professes knowledge to an senseless one; therefore, he is remembered as Vāgduṣṭa.
Constantly, through an attitude of atheism, toward the ancestors, gods, and men,

this sinner has no respect, nor for good deeds; therefore, he is Vidaivata.
Always begging falsely, falsely showing poverty,

troubling beings, greedy; therefore, he is this Yācanaka.
Having suffered the torments of hell due to these sins done in the past,

we ghosts, from your sight today, have been reborn and are well-established.
All this has been told to you, arising from our own history.

I wish to hear from you in truth about your food as well."
The ghosts said:
"Hear of our food, condemned by all creatures,

hearing which, O holy man, you will constantly revile us again and again:
With phlegm, urine, and feces, and with the bodily dirt of women,

houses where purification has been abandoned—there indeed they feed.
[Houses] ruined by women, disordered, and strewn with iron utensils,

and filthy with dirt—the ghosts indeed feed there.
Where they do not worship Mādhava, and houses overcome by women,

devoid of compassion and forbearance—there only do the ghosts feed.
Where ill words are spoken in the house, and women are devoid of purity,

and where quarrel is constant—the ghosts feed there.
In whose home sisters and noble women are not honored,

and where there is company with evil men—there we will eat.
Where there is neither service of Hari nor Vaiṣṇava narration,

nor Vaiṣṇava affection—the ghosts indeed feed there.
Delighted in the house of those people, they also eat swiftly;

and [the householders] become ghosts through that sin, destroyers of their own lineage.
To me speaking of my own food, O holy man, [loathing] arises;

nothing can be said to be more sinful than this.
Wearied by the condition of a ghost, I ask you of firm vows

how a ghost is not born, and how there is liberation from ghosthood."
The brahmin said:
"By meritorious vows such as Ekādaśī, by chanting the names of Acyuta,

by worship of deities and guests, and likewise by worship of the guru and others,
by righteous conduct, good deeds, and days enjoined by Śruti and Smṛti,

likewise by ancestral rites and gifts performed according to rule,
by compassion, generosity, self-restraint, forbearance, good conduct, and saluting the virtuous—

By these and other pious deeds, ghosts would not exist even in one's family:
[honoring] cows, brāhmaṇas, sacred bathing places, gods, prominent mountains, rivers and streams, and holy fig trees many times over.
The man who, disciplined, bows to his kinsmen never becomes a ghost in this world; / how much more so the disciplined man who worships them in due order!
At sacred bathing places such as the Gaṅgā, his merit is endless; / even the almighty Lord himself could not recount it in a thousand years.
Even by merely seeing him, one is freed from the state of a ghost. / Now [consider] the month of Ūrja, full of energy, beloved of Dāmodara,
the best month for austerities, penance dear to Mādhava; / [and] the month of Vaiśākha, Mādhava, having Madhusūdana as its deity,
which alone the sages know to be the best of all months; / by that very means, indeed, all duties are accomplished.
It is regarded as knowledge of Brahman; she is Lakṣmī, the maker of the universe; / since it is her dwelling place, this month is therefore called Mādhava.
Just as it is certain that among the gods there is no deity equal to Mādhava, / so among all the months there is no month dear to Mādhava [like this one].
Even having heard the glorification of that month of Mādhava with devotion, / one is released from birth as a ghost—what then of performing its rites?
Just from speaking with the virtuous, from resorting to sacred bathing places, / from reciting 'Nārāyaṇa,' and even from hearing his name,
a person devoted to bhakti is freed from all sins. / Therefore, O ghosts, I will strive for your liberation as well.
For the merit born of helping others cannot be attained even by sacrifices. / O ghosts, I shall therefore go to bathe in the waters of the Revā in the month of Mādhava,
when the sun is in Aries, followed by these men. / Those five [ghosts], who had accumulated sins through delusion,
came to bathe solely at my compassionate word.
'Meanwhile, by my command, remain right there in the forest without sorrow, / while I go to the waters of the blessed Narmadā, and setting aside the rite of my own bath,
I make figures of men of kuśa grass here in the Narmadā named after you, / and according to the rules, bound by compassion, I immerse the wretched ones in the month of Mādhava.'
In this way, within just three days, your release from birth as ghosts / will come through the mere bath of the kuśa-effigies, without doubt.
Nārada said: / Thus addressed, Muniśarman, honoured by those who placed their trust [in him], / went on, followed by those five.
Having gone there and then bathed in the morning, performing the rite as prescribed, / he bathed those ghosts made of kuśa grass in their names.
Remembered by the sage at the sacred bathing place, and thus bathed by name / by that meritorious man, the ghosts instantly became liberated and went to heaven.
As soon as those five sinners were submerged in the waters of the Revā by his word / in the holy month of Mādhava, their discoloured bodies at once attained the singular radiance of gold.
Made to hear the hymn that quells sins by Muniśarman, / in the presence of all the people, they took on excellent splendour.
The men standing there, however, did not touch them who had become spotless by the mere bath, / O king of kings, out of fear of contact with sinners.
Then, at the insistence of Muniśarman and by the authority of dharma, / immediately a heavenly voice arose: 'Since these have become free from sin,
for those who have bathed in the month of Mādhava, their hearts fixed on Mukunda, / hearing here with reverence the hymn that quells sins,
what wonder is there that purification arises from the accumulation of sins? / For this is the supreme expiation of all sins,
namely, plunging with devotion into a sacred bathing place in the morning during the month of Mādhava. / Since those sinful ghosts were bathed merely by name,
remembered by that meritorious Muniśarman, they were liberated.'

Having thus heard that most wondrous voice from the sky, the people immediately thereafter
praised those five meritorious ones, the month of Vaiśākha, the sage, and the Revā.
And then, O king, hear the praise that destroys sins, / hearing which with devotion, a person is freed from masses of sins,
by the mere hearing of which sinners have attained purification, / and many others too have been freed from sin born of ignorance.
When the mind of men inclines toward another's wife, another's wealth, harming living beings, and the like, / the hymn is then their expiation:
Homage to Viṣṇu, to Viṣṇu, always to Viṣṇu, to Viṣṇu! / I bow to Viṣṇu who is in the mind, to Hari who is within the sense of 'I',
to the Lord who is in the mind, unmanifest, infinite, unconquered, / to Viṣṇu who is to be praised by all beings, without beginning or end, the all-pervading.
Viṣṇu is that which is in my mind, Viṣṇu is that which is in my intellect, / and Viṣṇu is the ego; Viṣṇu is he who abides in me.
He acts, being the agent of both the motionless and the moving; / that sin comes to destruction when he alone is meditated upon.
He who, meditated upon, removes sin, and who is seen in a dream through contemplation— / to that Upendra, the great Viṣṇu, who is fond of bowing, I bow.
In this world devoid of support, toward Madhusūdana, Acyuta, / this hymn is a supporting hand; I praise Viṣṇu, the highest of the high.
O sovereign of all lords, O all-pervading one, O Supreme Self, O Adhokṣaja, / O Hṛṣīkeśa, O Hṛṣīkeśa, O Hṛṣīkeśa, homage to you!
O Nṛsiṃha, O Ananta, O Govinda, O source of all beings, O Keśava, / quell the sin that has been wrongly spoken, ill-done, or contemplated; homage to you!
Whatever wicked thought was meditated upon by me, subject to my own mind, / whatever wrong deed, very terrible sin, bring that to an end, O Keśava!
O god who loves the brāhmaṇas, O Govinda, devoted to the supreme truth, / O Lord of the universe, O supporter of the universe, quell my sin, O Acyuta!
And whatever sin has been done in the afternoon, in the evening, at noon, and at night, / by body, mind, or speech, unwittingly,
and knowingly, O Hṛṣīkeśa, O lotus-eyed one, O Mādhava, / by the utterance of the three names, may all [sins] come to destruction for me!
May my bodily sin, O Hṛṣīkeśa, my mental sin, O lotus-eyed one, / and that committed by speech, come to an end, O Mādhava!

Whatever sin I have committed for the sake of wealth while eating, drinking, standing,
sleeping, waking, or seated, by body, mind, or speech—
whether great or small, likely leading to bad rebirths and hell, / may that sin come to an end through the chanting of Vāsudeva!
That which is the supreme Brahman, the supreme abode, and the highest purity— / when that Viṣṇu is chanted, may whatever sin there is perish!
Reaching which, devoid of smell, touch, and the like, the wise / do not return—that highest step of Viṣṇu, may it quell all this!
Whatever man recites or listens to this hymn that quells sins / is released from sins committed by body, mind, and speech.
Freed from evil planets and the like, he goes to the supreme step of Viṣṇu. / Therefore, when a sin is committed, this hymn, destroying all sins, should be recited.
As an expiation for floods of sins, it should be recited by the best of men. / Sin is destroyed through expiations, excellent hymns, and vows.
Therefore, for full success, these should be performed for the sake of enjoyment and liberation. / The sin accumulated in a previous birth and that of this present life, O lord of men,
melts away at once from hearing this praise. / An axe to the tree of sins, a forest fire to the fuel of wickedness,
a sun to the dense darkness of heaps of sin is this praise, O king; / it has been revealed by me to you out of compassion for the world.
This hymn, a secret which was obtained by me from my father with reverence— / whatever king hears this holy legendary history,
Even Hari himself is scarcely able to express its holy greatness. / May there be welfare to you, O great king; I will now quickly go to the Gaṅgā,
to bathe, for this great month of Mādhava has arrived.

5.95.m: Sūta said: / Then, having bowed to the sage who was preparing to leave, the king joyfully / asked about the brief ritual proper for the rites of bathing and gifting.
Ambarīṣa said: / O sage, in this month of Vaiśākha, what is the rule? What is the higher austerity? / And what gift [should be given]? How should bathing be done, and how the worship of Keśava?
Tell me out of compassion, O brahmin sage; you are omniscient and dear to Hari. / In particular, tell me the rule of worship at a sacred place.
Nārada said: / When the sun enters Aries, O best of men, in the month of Mādhava, / in a great river, on a riverbank, in a river, in a lake, at a cascade,
or in a deity's reservoir, or in any pool of water that is found, / in oblong ponds, wells, or cisterns, one should bathe with a restrained mind, remembering Hari.
Having fasted on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Madhu, / or on the fifteenth day, O hero, or even upon the sun’s transit into Aries,
one should undertake the observance of the Vaiśākha bath with the permission of brahmins, / having worshipped Madhusūdana after bathing well.
"For the entire month of Vaiśākha, during the sun’s transit into Aries, / I shall bathe in the morning with self-restraint; may Madhusūdana be pleased."
"By the grace of the slayer of Madhu, and through the favor of the brahmins, / may my holy daily bath of Vaiśākha be free of obstacles."
"In the month of Mādhava, while the sun is in Aries, O Murāri, O Madhusūdana, / O Lord, through my morning bath become the giver of the fruit as declared."
"Just as the month of Mādhava is dear to you, O Madhusūdana, / through my morning bath in this [month], become the destroyer of sins and granter of fruits."
Having spoken thus, having washed both feet at that sacred place and restrained his speech, / remembering the divine Nārāyaṇa, he should perform the bath according to the rule.
The wise man should consecrate the holy water, reciting this root mantra: / "Namo Nārāyaṇāya" is declared to be the root mantra.
With darbha grass in hand, having sipped water according to the rule and bowed down on the ground, / having marked out a square measuring four cubits on all sides,
the person should invoke the Gaṅgā with this mantra: / "You were born from Viṣṇu's foot; you belong to Viṣṇu, having Viṣṇu as your deity.
Protect us from that sin committed from birth until death. / Thirty-five million sacred waters, Vāyu has declared,
exist in heaven, on earth, and in the atmosphere—they are present in you, O Jāhnavī! / Your name is Nandinī, and in the Vedas it is Nalinī,
Dakṣā, Pṛthvī, Vihagā, Viśvagāthā, Śivapriyā, / Vidyādharī, Mahādevī, and Lokaprasādinī,
Kṣemaṅkarī, Jāhnavī, Śāntā, and Śāntipradāyinī." / One should recite these sacred names at the time of bathing.
The Gaṅgā who flows along three paths will then become present there. / With water consecrated by chanting seven times and held in the hollow of folded hands,
placing it upon his head four, five, or seven times, O king, / and having bathed, he should likewise invoke the clay according to rule:
"O earth, traversed by horses, traversed by chariots, traversed by Viṣṇu! / O clay, take away my sin, whatever misdeed has been done by me.
You were lifted up by the Boar, by the hundred-armed Viṣṇu. / Salutations to you, O source of all worlds, O faithful one!"
Having bathed in this way, he should then sip water according to rule, / and rising, put on two pure white garments.
Then he should indeed offer water-libations for the gratification of the three worlds: / first he should satiate Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Prajāpati,
the gods, yakṣas, nāgas, gandharvas, apsarases, asuras, / cruel serpents, suparṇas, trees, insects, and birds,
the vidyādharas, clouds, and those who move through the sky, / and those souls that are without support and engaged in sinful deeds:
"For their satisfaction, water is offered by me." / A man should wear the sacred thread over the left shoulder for the gods, and wear it suspended around the neck [for human beings].
He should satiate with devotion human beings, the sons of Brahmā, and the sages: / Sanaka, Sanandana, and thirdly Sanātana.
“as well as Kapila, Āsuri, Voḍhu, and Pañcaśikha. / May they all be satisfied forever with the water given by me.”
To Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, / Pracetas, Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, and Nārada—

one should offer libations to all the divine and brāhmaṇa seers with water and unhusked barley. / Then one should put [the sacred thread] over the right shoulder, placing the right knee upon the ground.
The Agniṣvāttas, the Saumyas, the Haviṣmats, the Uṣmapās, / the Kavyānalas, the Barhiṣads, and also the Ājyapās—
one should satisfy the ancestors with devotion using water mixed with sesame and sandal paste. / “To Yama, to Dharmarāja, to Mṛtyu, and to Antaka,
to Vaivasvata, to Kāla, and to Sarvabhūtakṣaya, / to Uḍumbara, to Dadhna, to Nīla, to Parameṣṭhin,
to Vṛkodara, to Citra, and to Citragupta—homage indeed!” / Then, holding darbha grass in hand, he should satisfy the ancestors in accordance with the rules.
The father and other forebears by their names and gotras, and likewise maternal grandfathers— / having satisfied all according to rule, he should utter this mantra:
“Those who are kin, those who are not kin, and those who were kin in another life— / may all those who desire water from us find complete satisfaction.”
Having duly sipped water as prescribed, he should draw a lotus before him; / with unhusked barley, flowers, water, and red sandalwood,
he should carefully present the guest-offering, reciting the names of the Sun: / “Homage to you who are of the form of Viṣṇu, homage to you who are of the form of Brahmā,
homage to you the thousand-rayed Sun, homage to all your splendor! / Homage to you who have the form of Rudra, homage to you who are fond of your devotees!
Lotus-navelled one, homage to you, adorned with ear-rings and armlets! / Homage to you, lord of all the worlds, awakener of the sleeping!
You see good deeds and bad deeds, everything, at all times. / Homage to you, true deity; be pleased with me, light-maker!
Day-maker, homage to you! Maker of illumination, homage to you!” / Having thus paid homage to the Sun, circumambulating him seven times,
and having touched a twice-born, a cow, and gold, he should afterward go to his home. / Then, having honored those abiding in the hermitage, he should also worship the image.
First, with devotion, the self-controlled householder / should faithfully worship Govinda in both places according to rule, O king.
Especially in the month of Vaiśākha, whoever worships Madhusūdana, / by him Mādhava is worshipped for an entire year.
When the month of Mādhava has arrived and the witness of deeds is in Aries, / he should undertake the collection of Keśava-vows for the pleasure of Keśava.
He should give various gifts, such as sesame and clarified butter, / which bring an end to sins born of tens of millions of lifetimes.
Water, food, sugar, cows, and cows made of sesame— / gifts should be given according to one’s wealth for the attainment of the desired end.
Bathing daily through the entire month of Vaiśākha, senses conquered, / reciting prayers and eating sacrifical food, one is freed from all sins.
Eating once a day, or at night, or of unbegged food, unwearied— / whoever performs this in the month of Mādhava obtains all that he desires.
In Vaiśākha, duly taking two baths outside in a river and the like, / sacrificial food, celibacy, sleeping on the ground, observance of restrictions,
a vow, gift, recitation, oblation, and worship of Madhusūdana / burn away terrible sin, even that arising from a thousand births.
Just as Mādhava, when meditated upon, destroys taint, / even so does bathing performed according to rule in the month of Mādhava.
Daily bathing at a sacred ford, ancestral libation with sesame seeds, / giving of jars of dharma and other gifts, and worship of Madhusūdana—
these should be performed in the month of Mādhava, giving pleasure to Madhusūdana. / Water with sesame, gold, food, sugar, garments, ornaments,
footwear, umbrellas, and water jars should be given to twice-born persons. / With devotion at the three twilights he should worship the Lord, Madhusūdana,
who is directly accompanied by spotless Lakṣmī, with concentrated mind. / And [he should gratify] many brāhmaṇas with vessels of gold and sesame to the best of his ability.
Whoever satisfies [them] with water jars removes the sin of killing a brāhmaṇa. / Having bathed in the morning in a river in the month of Vaiśākha, composed in mind,
and having worshipped Hari with devotion using seasonal flowers and fruits, / he should worship a brāhmaṇa according to his capacity, avoiding conversation with heretics.
He should satisfy [them] with gifts of garments, cows, riches such as jewels. / As for other wealth, he should offer it little by little according to his ability.
Afterwards, a man destitute of wealth, in the month of Mādhava, / should worship Mādhava, Madhusūdana, by the rite of offering flowers.
Liberated from all sins, he delivers a hundred ancestors; / for a hundred thousand lives he does not experience grief as a result.
He has no fear of disease, no poverty, no bondage; / he is born in birth after birth as a devotee of Viṣṇu, fortunate.
For as many as one hundred and eight thousands of yugas / he lives in heaven, O hero, and becomes an earthly king again.
Having enjoyed the diverse pleasures of a king as he pleases, / by the grace of Mādhava he then merges into Mādhava.
Listen, O king, I will explain in brief the worship of Mādhava, / Vedic, Tantric, or mixed, which destroys sin.
For there is no end to the boundless, nor an end to the rite of worship, O king; / hence it will be stated in brief, in proper order as it should be.
The worship of glorious Viṣṇu is of three kinds: Vedic, Tantric, and mixed; / by whichever of the three is desired, one should worship Hari.
The Vedic or the mixed is prescribed for the twice-born and others; / the Tantric is proclaimed for a devotee of Viṣṇu, even for a śūdra.
Having attained twice-born status, as stated in his own Vedic text, / a celibate student, collected in mind, should sacrifice to Viṣṇu according to rule.
One should worship in a cleared space, or in fire, in the sun, in water, in the heart, or in a twice-born, / with devotion, using materials, along with his guru by the guru’s permission.
First, he should take a bath, having cleaned his teeth, for the purification of his limbs. / Bathing of both [internal and external] is done with mantras, taking up clay and the like.
After the twilight worship and other duties declared in the Vedas and Tantras, / at the conclusion of worship he should duly form a pure resolve for the rite.
Of stone, of wood, of iron, of plaster, painted, of sand, / made of mind, and made of jewels: an image is recognized to be of eight kinds.
The temple of life is twofold in its installation: movable and immovable. / In the worship of Mādhava, there is dismissal and invocation for an immovable one.
For an immovable one there may be an option, but in a cleared space both apply. / There is bathing for an unplastered image, but in other cases wiping clean.
Worship of the gods in images and the like is done with known substances by an honest devotee, / and with whatever is obtained, with devotional disposition.
Bathing and decorating are paramount only in an image, O king; / in cleared spaces, arranging [the deities]; in fire, sacrificial food offered with clarified butter.
In the sun, offering homage is best; in a cleared space, with water and the like; / offered with faith to Hari by a devotee, even water is supreme.
How much more so perfume, incense, flowers, a lamp, and food! / Pure, having gathered the requisites, with a seat prepared with darbha grass facing east,
seated facing east or north, or facing opposite the image, / having performed the placement of mantras, he should touch with his hand the image of Hari upon which placement has been done.
He should properly prepare a pot and sprinkling water; / with that water, he should sprinkle the place of divine sacrifice, the articles, and himself.
Having sprinkled three vessels with water, he should set them down with the various materials; / he should provide three vessels for the water for washing feet, the guest-offering, and sipping water.

He should consecrate them with the heart mantra, the head mantra, the tuft mantra, and the Gāyatrī. / When the physical body has been purified by breath and fire, [one should meditate upon] the supreme part of the all-pervading Lord situated in the lotus of the heart,

subtle, the vital digit, meditated upon at the end of the primordial sound, realized by perfection. / When the body is pervaded by that which has become one’s self, having worshipped, absorbed in Him,

having invoked Him and established Him in an image or the like, with the limbs placed upon it, he should worship Him; / he should arrange offerings such as water for washing feet, the guest-offering, bathing, and adoration.
Having arranged Hari's seat with the nine [principles] beginning with dharma, / and upon it an eight-petaled lotus gleaming with pericarp and filaments,
by both Vedic and Tantric methods for the attainment of both [goals] from Hari, / one should worship Sudarśana, Pāñcajanya, the mace, arrow, bow, plough,
pestle, Kaustubha jewel, garland, and the Śrīvatsa mark; / Nanda, Sunanda, Garuḍa, Pracaṇḍa, and Caṇḍa,
Mahābala, Bala, Kumuda, Kumudekṣaṇa, / Durgā, Vināyaka, Vyāsa, Viṣvaksena, the gurus, and the gods.
Facing them in their respective places, he should worship them with sprinkling and other rites; / with waters scented with sandalwood, vetiver, camphor, saffron, and agallochum,
he should bathe Him with mantras daily, or when means are available: / with the Svarṇagharma hymn, the Mahāpuruṣa formula,
the Puruṣasūkta hymn, Sāman chants, waving of lights, and other rites. / With garments, sacred thread, ornaments, leaves, garlands, and scented unguents,
the devotee of Viṣṇu should lovingly adorn Him in a suitable manner. / Water for washing feet, water for sipping, fragrance, blossoms, unbroken grains,
incense, perfume, and offerings the worshipper should give with faith: / jaggery, milk rice, clarified butter, pastries, cakes, and sweet dumplings.
He should offer an oblatory meal of milk rice, curd, and clarified butter; / anointing with oil, rubbing the body, mirror, tooth-cleaning stick, and ceremonial bath,
food and so forth, dancing, and songs should all be offered daily. / In a pit constructed according to rule, with tiered rings, an altar, and a girdle,
having established the fire, he should sweep the water around with his hand; / having spread [darbha grass] around, sprinkled it with water, and placed the sacrificial fuel according to rule,

having placed the offerings with the sprinkling vessel, and sprinkling clarified butter with the same sprinkling vessel, / [meditating on Him] resembling molten Jāmbūnada gold, with conch, discus, mace, and lotus,
splendid with four arms, peaceful, clad in garments yellow as lotus filaments, / with a flashing crown, bracelets, a waist-cord, and excellent armlets,
with the Śrīvatsa on His chest, resplendent with the Kaustubha jewel, wearing a forest garland; / meditating on Him, worshipping the wood, and with sacrificial offerings mixed with clarified butter,

having cast the two portions of clarified butter and the two Āghāra oblations, and offered the oblation inundated with clarified butter, / having worshipped and saluted, he should present the offering to the attendants.
He should chant the root mantra, O brahmin, remembering that it consists of Nārāyaṇa; / having offered water for sipping, he should assign the remnants of the offering to Viṣvaksena.
He should offer fragrant mouth-perfume, betel and the like, / singing and reciting constantly [the Lord's] deeds with loud voices.
Relating and hearing edifying stories, he should remain for a short time, / [praising him] with diverse hymns and eulogies, both Purāṇic and in the vernacular.
Having praised him with, 'Be gracious, O Blessed One!' he should prostrate like a stick, / placing his head at his feet with both arms crossed,
[saying,] 'I have taken refuge; protect me, O Lord, terrified of the ocean of the crocodile of death!' / Having respectfully placed upon his head the remnants offered to Hari,

he should dismiss [him] if he is to be dismissed, [uniting] the light within his own light. / Where a faithful person has fixed his devotion, whether in an icon or other forms, there he should worship.
[He should worship] the Self of all residing in all beings and in himself. / Thus a man, by paths of practical yoga, both Vedic and Tantric,
who worships Hari, attains from him the desired perfection. / Having duly consecrated that icon, he should cause a sturdy temple to be built,
with delightful flower gardens, worship, processions, festivals, and the like, / in order to maintain the continuous flow of worship and other rites on great festival days and daily.
By granting fields, shops, towns, and villages, he attains union [with Hari]. / By consecration [he gains the status of] a sovereign emperor; by [building] a temple, the three worlds;
by worship and other services, the world of Brahmā; by all three, he attains equality with him. / Through devotion that is free from desire, he attains him alone.
that intellect is white as a spotless moon and conch, which pervades Mādhava; / that tongue is sweet-speaking, O king, which repeatedly praises Nārāyaṇa.
Worship should also be performed by women and Śūdras using the basic mantra, / and by others with faith according to the path taught by their own guru, O Vaiṣṇava.
All this purifying worship of Mādhava has been told to you. / Do this especially in the month of Mādhava, O lord of the earth.
Sūta said: / Having heard these wonderful, meritorious, and purifying words of the son of Brahmā, / the king, foremost among the devotees of the Lord, bowed with joined palms and spoke eagerly:

Ambarīṣa said: / I am the lord of the entire circle of the earth, my commands unimpeded, a server of the wise, / my mind surrendered to the lotus feet of Govinda, having pleased the brāhmaṇas with my heart;
a renowned jewel of a royal lineage, constant in delight for dharma, famous, / endowed with beauty, valor, and the virtue of generosity, blessed with virtuous sons, my foes conquered;

by what merit was I born with a pure intellect, endowed with such virtues and glory? / Moreover, from where did I obtain this lovely wife, glowing with beauty, like Lakṣmī herself, the embodiment of merit?
Explain to me fully all this good deed practiced by me in a previous birth, / O sage; you are omniscient, an ocean of compassion.
Nārada said: / She who is now your very beautiful wife of truthful conduct / was in another birth a courtesan named Rūpavatī.
The noble woman lived by the duty prescribed for a courtesan, / performing indeed auspicious deeds at the instruction of a brāhmaṇa.
You were a goldsmith celebrated by the name Devadāsa; / in that previous birth, you were her lover, her paramour.
She served you eagerly, beautiful Rūpavatī; / and she adhered to the highest knowledge, the path of dharma for the sake of expending wealth.
Once, hearing the duty arising from the bath in the month of Vaiśākha, / that pious woman took a bath in the water when the sun had entered Aries.
The capable courtesan Rūpavatī constantly gave gifts, / offering salutations to a brāhmaṇa with devotion and respect.
Enjoined by her affection, you, as that Devadāsa, were awakened by her, / and reverently took the bath in the month of Mādhava with proper understanding.
There, on the pure third lunar day at the beginning of the Tretā age, / she respectfully said to that goldsmith Devadāsa:
The courtesan said: / Make an excellent golden image of Madhusūdana, Acyuta. / Having worshipped the god with barley grains and satisfied the fire with them,
I shall give it to a brāhmaṇa with the permission of brāhmaṇas. / In the Purāṇas, this gift given at that time is said to be inexhaustible.
I have heard from brāhmaṇas that that bright third lunar day / of the month of Vaiśākha is called Akṣayā, which grants inexhaustible fruit.
On this day, I will give that golden, imperishable Madhusūdana. / Nārada said: / Hearing her sweet words, the goldsmith,
free from deceit, for the sake of dharma, with a truthful disposition, / made a beautiful golden image of Acyuta,
and an image endowed with auspicious characteristics, as prescribed, of the moon; / having bathed according to rule, she gave that beautiful [image] to a brāhmaṇa,
having worshipped it, O king, on that Akṣayā tithi.
After some time, that courtesan, steadfast in dharma, died; / and Devadāsa also died constantly at the exhaustion of his lifespan.
By that merit, O king, the goldsmith in another birth / became you, O king, who obtained the earth, endowed with all virtues.
And that courtesan Rūpavatī, by that dharma, became yours— / your lovely wife named Kāntimatī, overflowing with affection.
Diverse are the latent impressions of past actions, O hero; / strange are their courses, dear one, not known even by the wise.
There is no doubt regarding the practice concerning this month of Mādhava; / it was kept hidden by that Lord, by Brahmā, and by Mādhava.

By those with bad company, who have not attained knowledge, who are undisciplined and devoid of the duty of the āśramas, / who have not visited holy fords and have performed no vows—by them the observance of the month of Mādhava is not attained.

Those on whose lips the excellent speech, 'Govinda, Keśava, Mukunda, Hari, Murāri, / Abode of Lakṣmī, Madhusūdana, Kṛṣṇa, Viṣṇu!' does not reside—to them the observance of the month of Vaiśākha does not belong.

Those who do not listen to virtuous words that are exceedingly beneficial, and to the nectarean deeds of Hari, / and who do not look upon the temples of the husband of Kamalā—they do not attain the observance of the month of Vaiśākha.

By whom gurus were not served, nor a maiden given in marriage, adorned, to a suitable groom at the proper time, / nor sons instructed in modesty and other virtues—they do not attain the observance of the month of Vaiśākha.

Sūta said: / Having thus instructed the king and bid him farewell, the sage, foremost of those who know mantras, / went to bathe in the Gaṅgā in the month of Mādhava, having then been worshipped by him, O brāhmaṇas.

Then that king too, of holy mind, celebrated throughout the world for his purifying fame, / performed the rite of the month of Vaiśākha taught by the sage, together with his wife, meditating on him alone.

5.96.m: The sages said: / Sūta, Sūta of great wisdom, live, live for a hundred years, / since we have been made to hear the auspicious season, beneficial to the world!
Speak even more abundantly! We drink your words; / drinking again and again that supreme [speech], we are not sated, O Sūta!
Sūta said: / Here too they cite this ancient legendary history, / the conversation of the primordial world, of the Lord of the worlds.
Six thousand [yojanas] in height, and three [thousand] in width; / thus, having made nine thousand yojanas,
Held by his left tusk, the earth was first lifted up; / indeed, the earth was supported on his tusk for a thousand divine years.
In the course of discussing dharma, she said with humility to the lord: / The Earth said: / “These twelve months indeed consist of three hundred and sixty days.
Among them, which is the most meritorious and dear to you, O Keśava? / The month of Kārtika is sacred when the sun is in Tulā.
The month when the sun is in Makara is traditionally regarded as purifying in the Purāṇa; / the month of Mādhava, when the sun is in Meṣa, is recited by the wise.
Mārgaśīrṣa also is proclaimed to be purifying among the months. / Thus are the sacred months; which days are proclaimed [likewise]?
The beginnings and ends of yugas, and likewise the beginnings of kalpas: / tell me of the purifying month that is superior even to all of these.
O glorious one, composed of all sacrifices, determine and tell me that one [month].” / The Boar said: / “Even according to the prescribed rules, those vile men who sacrifice,
if they worship me with devotion in the month of Mādhava, I am always to be worshipped by them. / O fair-hipped one, Hiraṇyākṣa was slain in [the month of] Mādhava, and Madhu too was slain.
Having slain both of these primordial daityas, you were rescued. / In the Tretā age, the threefold Vedic duty, knowledge, and the arrangement of castes
came into being in the month of Mādhava; therefore Mādhava is dear to me. / The Tretā age [began] on the third lunar day of the bright fortnight in the month of Mādhava;
it commenced, and the threefold Vedic duties commenced and flourished. / That third day is called inexhaustible (Akṣayā) in the world, beloved of Hari.
In bathing, giving gifts, worship, śrāddha, recitation of mantras, and libations to ancestors, / those who worship Viṣṇu with barley grains and perform the śrāddha with diligence—
to them I grant everything, whatever highest desire is in their hearts. / Those men who also give gifts are fortunate and righteous.
Those who constantly sacrifice to Hari with diverse rituals— / whoever sacrifices to me in Mādhava obtains a fruit greater than theirs.
Bathing, gift-giving, silent recitation, fire offerings, asceticism, sacrifices, vows, and the like: / hear the meritorious fruit of what is done in Vaiśākha, O goddess.
For seventeen crores of manvantaras, / they remain in my presence, free from fear.
Even if all planets should be cruel, in the house of birth, expense, or the eighth, / by bathing at dawn in Vaiśākha, they all become benign.
Whoever feeds brāhmaṇas in the month of Vaiśākha, intent on devotion, / for every morsel of food, there is satisfaction for the ancestors for the duration of a yuga.
Those who provide sweet foods in abundance, or meals of barley, and water with sesame seeds, / umbrellas, garments, and appropriate footwear—they alone are blessed, causing delight to Viṣṇu.
Especially here, sesame seeds mixed with honey should be given, / for the sake of great dharma and to cause the destruction of long-accumulated sins.
When this is done, the merit that is attained by those men— / by whom could it be calculated even in hundreds of millions of years?
Wealth of sons, grandsons, and the like, and a long life as desired, / he attains in this world, and in the next world he attains me alone.
The series of sins accumulated in many births dissolves through bathing in Mādhava, / or when a person takes shelter at dawn at a sacred pilgrimage place according to the injunction.
