He who, abandoning Vaiśākha, undertakes some other observance, / leaves a great jewel resting in his hand and begs for a clod of earth.”
Sūta said: / Thus the lord, the ancient foremost god, the bearer of the earth, / spoke formerly concerning the month of Mādhava upon the earth.
What is the use of saying much here? There is nothing, O earthly gods, / that cannot be obtained by worshipping Mādhava in the month of Mādhava.
Hear also an ancient event on this subject, supreme and wondrous: / the conversation between a brāhmaṇa and the great-souled Yama.
In the Madhyadeśa there was a great village of brāhmaṇas, / between the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā, below the Yamunā mountain.
Very many learned brāhmaṇas dwelt there at that time. / Then Yama spoke to a certain dark and reddish-brown man,
with red eyes, hair standing on end, and legs, eyes, and nose like a crow's: / “Go, sir, to that great village, and having gone, bring a brāhmaṇa
born in the Vasiṣṭha lineage, Yajñadatta by name, / established in tranquility, learned, and skilled in the sacrificial rites.
And do not bring another from his clan beside him, / who possesses the same qualities, equal to him in learning and birth,
and equal to him, the best of men, in form and bodily marks; / bring the one designated, for I must pay him worship.”
Going there, however, he acted contrary to Yama's command; / he brought that very one whom Yama had forbidden.
Rising to meet him and having worshipped him, Yama, knower of dharma, / said: “Let him be led away, and let that other one be brought.”
Sūta said: / When these words were spoken by Dharmarāja, that twice-born man, / unwilling to depart, spoke to Dharmarāja:
The brāhmaṇa said: / “Why was I brought here, and why do you send me back again? / I do not wish to go back to that mortal world, O lord.”
Yama said: / “Here is the abode of meritorious men whose lifespans are exhausted; / this indeed is the realm of Dharmarāja, proclaimed as righteousness itself.
All this is a place of happiness, and I, Dharmarāja, am the ruler, / granting pleasure and pain to creatures according to their merits and demerits.
For sinners I have the form of Yama, bestowing hell upon men; / likewise, for the virtuous, I am the embodiment of dharma, bestowing bliss and heaven.
Go, O brāhmaṇa, this very day to your own home, just as you came; / ten years of your lifespan still remain today.
When your lifespan is exhausted, you will attain this world; / and if anything else is to be asked by you, ask: I shall tell you.”
The brāhmaṇa said: / “Tell me that by doing which very great merit is gained, leading to heaven; / for you are the authority for all in determining dharma and adharma.
If, O god, I must properly return to my own house, / then tell me: by what action do men fall into hell?
And by what do they go to heaven? Tell all that out of compassion.” / Yama said: / “Those men who are averse to dharma in action, mind, and speech,
and those devoid of devotion to Viṣṇu, are indeed bound for hell. / Those who see Brahmā, Śaṃkara, and Hari with a mind of division,
and men who are detached from the sacred knowledge of Viṣṇu, are bound for hell. / One who abandons the duty suited to his family and country and performs another,
whether from desire or from delusion, that man goes to hell. / One who officiates for those unfit to sacrifice, and one who abandons those fit to sacrifice,
and one averse to the sacred knowledge of Viṣṇu—he suffers many hells. / Without giving to the ancestors, gods, and brāhmaṇas, or among mortal kin,
a wealthy man dies a sinner; he goes to many hells. / One who, when all the food is prepared, makes distinctions in the cooking,
and eats without having performed the vaiśvadeva rite, goes to hell for a long time. / Those who acquire wealth by great injury to living beings, O twice-born,
wealthy, hypocritical men bound for hell, partake of suffering. / Those who, out of disbelief, greed, or delusion, at the prescribed time,
do not offer śrāddha with devotion—they are boiled in hells. / But the evildoer [who obstructs] wealth being given to brāhmaṇas,”
The man who causes an obstacle to the wealth given to Brahmins goes to hell. / When a common sacrificial fee has been received, one who out of delusion takes it alone,
and the man intent on atheistic views will abide in hell. / By his intolerance toward the virtues [of others], a reason will arise
for a great sin to be born, which is a cause of hell. / He who in time abandons the faultless wife of his friends,
and does not maintain their fame—that man will fall into hell. / He who, under the sway of delusion, calls adharma dharma,
and the rationalizing skeptic who is an atheist—that man has his dwelling in hell. / He who thinks one way in his mind and speaks otherwise with his speech,
and makes his heart foul—that man will dwell in hell. / And those men who treat the singing of the Lord's praises with contempt,
they go to a terrible hell because of that sinful deed. / Those who, seeing the Lord's doorway, his names, scriptures, and sacred attire,
do not offer obeisance and the like, go to dwell in hell. / Men who, without any fault, marry another wife over their first wife,
and those who abandon a virtuous wife—those men go to hell. / A man who does not listen to the word of his guru or to the dharmaśāstra,
and causes distress to the minds of others, will go to hell. / One who greedily eats sweet food while his relatives and children are watching,
merely filling his own belly, goes to a terrible hell. / He who does not perform the morning bath when the sun is in Libra, Capricorn, and Aries,
and is skeptical regarding rivers and the like, will have his abode in hell. / He who, having seen a Vaiṣṇava, does not rise to greet him,
out of love and respect, O Brahmin, that man is a guest of hell. / Those who block roads with pieces of wood, stakes,
spears, or even stones, certainly go to hell. / Those who do not think upon Viṣṇu, the primeval person, the Lord,
the great master of all the worlds, certainly go to hell. / Those men who cut off a field, a livelihood, or a home, or sever affection,
and cut off hope—those men are dwellers in hell. / When Brahmins worn down by their livelihood have arrived for a meal,
the foolish-minded person who interrogates them should be known as a guest of hell. / When a Vaiṣṇava is destitute, miserable, afflicted by disease, or old,
the fools who have no compassion for him certainly go to hell. / Those who, having undertaken religious vows, afterward fail to control their senses
and repeatedly violate them, certainly go to hell. / Listen, O Brahmin, how compassionate men go to heaven.
I shall tell you in brief, out of some respect for you. / Those who worship the god Hari, the victorious, eternal Viṣṇu,
Nārāyaṇa, the unborn, Kṛṣṇa, Viṣvaksena, four-armed, / who meditate on the divine person and remember Acyuta,
attain the abode of Acyuta; such is the ancient revelation. / For this alone is auspiciousness; this alone is the acquisition of wealth;
and this is the fruit of life: singing the praise of Dāmodara. / From praising the God of gods, Viṣṇu of immeasurable splendor,
sins dissolve away just as darkness does at sunrise. / Those who daily sing a Vaiṣṇava hymn endowed with faith,
constantly intent on sacred study—those men go to heaven. / Those who, casting aside all afflictions, praise Viṣṇu alone,
constant in their own duty and steadfast—those men go to heaven. / Even towards people who have committed sin, if they are devoted to the recitation of Vāsudeva's name,
the terrible messengers of Yama do not approach them, O Brahmin. / For living beings, they see no other atonement that calms all sins
than singing the praise of Hari, O best of the twice-born. / Those who rejoice when asked, give and speak kindly,
and renounce the fruit of their gift—those men go to heaven. / Men who avoid sleeping by day, and who endure everything,
and who offer shelter on sacred days—those mortals go to heaven. / Those who never speak of the faults even of their enemies,
and proclaim their virtues instead—those men go to heaven. / Those who, seeing the prosperity of others, are not tormented by envy,
but are delighted and applaud—those men go to heaven. / In the path of active engagement and of renunciation, what is stated in the Veda and the scriptures,
those who faithfully respect it—those men go to heaven. / In whatever family they may be born, compassionate and renowned,
Those men who are compassionate and of good conduct go to heaven; / those who are pure, and do not delight in the wives of others
in action, thought, or speech, being established in goodness, go to heaven; / those who always perform rites as prescribed and execute what is ordained,
having understood their own capacity, those men go to heaven. / Whoever constantly has faith in dharma of mind, speech, and body,
and is approved by the virtuous, becomes a guest of the gods. / He who endures the urge of speech, the urge of the mind, the urge arising from the belly,
and the urge of the genitals—that man is born in heaven. / Those whose contentment lies in virtues, whose speech is directed toward sacred learning,
and whose intellect is fixed on the supreme truth—those cultured men go to heaven. / Those who guard their vow from anger, who guard prosperity from envy,
learning from honor and dishonor, and the self from carelessness, / who guard the intellect from greed, and the mind from lust,
and guard dharma from bad company—those men go to heaven. / Those devoted to fasting in the proper manner on the eleventh lunar day,
in both the bright and dark fortnights, O brahmin, those men go to heaven. / Like a mother to all children, like medicine to the sick,
the eleventh lunar day was created for the protection of all the worlds. / There is no protection equal to the eleventh lunar day;
having fasted on it according to the rule, men go to heaven. / Whatever sin has been committed by the eleven senses, O twice-born,
having shaken that off swiftly, a man goes to heaven with delight. / Thousands of horse sacrifices and hundreds of Rājasūya sacrifices
are not worth a sixteenth part of a fast on the eleventh lunar day. / On one side are all the sacrifices and austerities at all sacred places,
gifts such as the great gifts—and on the other side is the Vaiṣṇava vow. / The dharma born of the Vaiṣṇava vow and the dharma produced by sacrifices and the like:
when weighed together by the Creator, the former is heavier. / For devotees of the day of Hari, who speak the names of Acyuta and Ananta,
I am not the punisher; in fact, O brahmin, I am afraid of them. / He whose son and grandson have fasted on the eleventh lunar day
forcibly delivers a hundred men along with himself. / Therefore, one should observe fasting on both fortnights;
on the eleventh lunar day, that man becomes the sole vessel of enjoyment and liberation. / Jayā, Vijayā, and Jayantī, destroying sins,
Trispṛśā, Vañjulī, the excellent Pakṣasaṃvardhinī, / the supreme Tiladugdhā, and likewise Akhaṇḍadvādaśī,
the one called Manorathā, and also the Bhīmadvādaśī— / such are the many varieties of the twelfth lunar day.
Those who are capable in these vows should be known as established in Brahman. / Those who listen to the treatises on dharma, joined with faith in dharma,
and who do good to children—they go to the world of heaven. / Men observing the vow of ancestral rites on the new moon, one day each month,
whose ancestors are gratified—they are blessed and go to heaven. / When meals are prepared, those who respectfully offer food
with an unchanged countenance—those cultured men go to heaven.
Those who have devotion to Madhusūdana, to Nārāyaṇa the lord of all, / even if devoid of truth and joined with passion, go to heaven with endless merit.
Those of auspicious conduct, devoted to bathing and giving gifts, / who resort to the Vitastā, the Yamunā, the Sītā, and the holy Godāvarī river,
never see the path of hell. / Those who bathe here in the Narmadā, the giver of happiness, or are pleased even by seeing it,
having shaken off their sins, go to the world of the Great Lord and delight there for a long time.
Restrained men who have bathed on the bank of the Carmanvatī river for three nights, / especially at Vyāsa's hermitage, are remembered as dwellers in heaven.
Those who have died in the water of the Gaṅgā, at Prayāga, at Kedāra, Puṣkara, / at Vyāsa's hermitage, and at Prabhāsa, go to Viṣṇu.
Those who have died at Dvāravatī, at Kurukṣetra, or through the practice of yoga, / and those who have the syllable 'Hari' on their mouth, do not have rebirth.
Those who have stayed even for three nights in the city of Dvāravatī, O brahmin, / and bathe on the bank of the Gomatī, are blessed and dear to Keśava.
Those who take refuge for three nights at the abode of Nara and Nārāyaṇa / in the mortal world, and at the Nandā, are blessed and dear to Keśava.
Having dwelt for six months near Puruṣottama, O brahmin, / they become united with Acyuta and, having seen him, surely have their sins removed.
Those who, by holy waters earned through many births, bathe in the waters of Maṇikarṇikā, / and having reached Kāśī bow to the Lord of the Universe, are indeed to be revered even by me here.
Having worshipped Hari with kuśa grass and sesame seeds on the ground, / having scattered sesame seeds, and having given iron and a milch cow,
those men who have died according to the proper manner, O brahmin, go to heaven. / Having fathered sons and established them in the paternal and ancestral position,
those who die devoid of selfishness and egoism also become dwellers in heaven. / Those continually turned away from theft, contented with their own wealth,
who live off their own fortune—those men go to heaven. / Those who speak gentle words that cause no affliction and are free from deceitful sweet means,
addressing others with a welcome—those men go to heaven. / Those who understand the maturation of the accumulation of fruits
of both good and bad deeds, O brahmin—those men go to heaven. / Those who foster the enthusiasm of those engaged in wealth and dharma,
and following the path of dharma—those men rejoice in heaven. / He who gives fire in winter, and likewise gives water in summer,
and gives shelter during the rains, rejoices for a long time in heaven. / At all auspicious times, during regular, occasional, and other occasions,
he who performs ancestral rites with devotion surely partakes of the world of the gods.

Gifts from a poor man, forgiveness from a powerful one, austerity of the young, silence of the wise, / restraint of desires in those accustomed to pleasure, and compassion toward living beings lead to heaven.
The connection of karma is twofold, arising from sin and merit; / relying upon truth alone, the decision is indeed made here.
Austerity combined with meditation is for crossing the ocean of worldly existence; / but sin is declared to cause a fall; this is the truth, without doubt.
Even for a man endowed with strength, retinue, and valor, / if he is devoid of merit, that strength and the rest will dissolve.
There are lofty, well-nourished trees in mountain strongholds; / yet, even though dense, they fall by the force of the wind along with their roots.
Likewise, those devoid of truth and dharma go to the abode of Yama. / Dharma is the common and sole strength for all living beings,
by which a creature crosses over in this world and the next. / All this that bestows the path to heaven has been duly
declared by me in brief. What more do you wish to hear?

5.97.m: The brahmin said: / Even a fool knows this: a man who performs auspicious deeds / does not go to hell, nor does one devoted to sinful acts go to heaven.
Heavenly happiness is attained through various sacrifices properly offered, vows, gifts, recitations, and the like, / and by those skilled in truthful conduct.
Heaven is sometimes attained through the conjunction of merit, by sages possessing learning, conduct, and wealth, / who have crossed to the further shore of the Vedas, through sacrifices;
and without wealth, one cannot give much in gifts, / even with wealth present, for one whose mind is attached to his family.
[they go to heaven]. The duties such as the agnihotra, especially in the Kali age, / are difficult to perform; the duty of giving gifts is also considered difficult to perform, O Lord.
An accumulation of dharma is attained by a duty involving little exertion. / Tell me that in detail, O revealer of dharma and adharma.
Let that one dharma, the most supreme among all dharmas, be declared, / by performing which alone all sin here is destroyed;
by which wealth, grain, renown, dharma, and lifespan increase, / there is friendship even in the mortal world, and heaven becomes imperishable;
by which Nārāyaṇa himself, who bestows fearlessness on his devotees, / is pleased, and by whose grace desire is placed in the palm of one's hand;
and by which a fruit greater than all sacrifices, austerities, gifts, and attendance on sacred fords / is attained—if there is such a thing, O son of Vivasvat, instruct me in it.
If I am indeed worthy of grace, O god, by instruction in dharma, / kindly tell me that one essential practice of all dharma.
Appropriate atonements for sins have been declared in various ways / by the wise, who called them to mind in accordance with each [offense].
Men are not able to perform them individually, O god. / If there is a single meritorious act that removes all sins, speak of it."
Sūta said: / Having spoken thus, that best of Brahmins, desiring subtle dharma, / became attentive and praised Yama, the embodiment of dharma:
The Brahmin said: / "Salutations to you, all-destroyer; salutations to the lord of the worlds! / Salutations to the one whose form is divine, who bestows the path to heaven!
Salutations to you, O Dharmarāja, whose nature is the dharmaśāstra! / By you, O god, the earth is protected, and the mid-region, heaven, and Maharloka;
Janarloka, Tapoloka, and Satyaloka—everything is protected by you. / There is nothing whatever in the world, unmoving or moving,
that is devoid of you. When seized by you, the world indeed instantly perishes. / You are the self of all beings, possessing the nature of sattva for the virtuous;
you are the rajas of those of passionate nature, and likewise the tamas of the ignorant. / You, O god, have four feet, four horns, three eyes,
seven hands, and are bound three ways: salutations to you in the form of the bull! / Dharma consisting of all sacrifices has its physical embodiment in you.
You have been seen directly, O ruler of the world, O god! Salutations, salutations to you! / Situated in the heart of all beings, you are the watcher of merits and sins;
therefore, O god, you are the punisher of beings, the giver [of fruit], the governor. / For you are the promoter of dharma, the wielder of the staff on earth.
State the one firmly ascertained essence that comprises all dharmas." / Yama said: / "I am well pleased with you, O Brahmin, especially by your praise.
Furthermore, by the traditional law, you are to be honored by me, O best of men. / That which has not been declared to anyone, that supreme secret of mine,
that single [truth] ascertained by me having extracted the essence of all things, / which supremely banishes one from the masses of great hells—
even though it should not be told, O Brahmin, pleased by your humility, I shall speak."

Those Purāṇas and scriptures may indeed bewilder the moving and unmoving world; / let them proclaim this or that deity as supreme in various ritual rules and eons, / but in the final conclusion the blessed Viṣṇu alone is determined [to be the supreme], / once the discriminatory intellect resolves the contradiction among all scriptural practices.
Bhava, Brahmā, and Viṣṇu: these three alone are considered the triad. / Just as a lamp is composed of fire, wick, and oil, O brāhmaṇa, so is Hari.
Having worshipped Hari with devotion, one attains the auspicious Goloka realms; / when Hari is worshipped, all desires rest in the palm of one's hand.
Giving alone is the highest and best among all merits, O twice-born; / through giving, sin is destroyed; through giving, everything is attained.
Regular, occasional, motivated, another for prosperity, / and another supreme: thus giving is traditionally known to be of five kinds.
Whatever little is given with effort in the three times of day— / morning, midday, and afternoon—is declared to be regular giving.
A day should not be made empty by those who desire their own benefit; / whatever is given in a family stands by them here and there.
He who, devoid of intellect, eats by himself through delusion without giving, / for him I produce disease, which puts an end to his enjoyment.
Afflicted with these ailments, causing much torment, / accompanied by sluggish digestive fire, an entrance causing great suffering.
Those by whom nothing was given to brāhmaṇas and gods at the three times of day, / and who eat sweet food for themselves, have indeed committed a great sin.
I purify them by means of terrible expiation, / with fasts, O earthly god, that dry up the body, and the like.
Just as a leather-worker ruthlessly purifies skin over a pit, / and treats it with a whip and other tools, bursting bad matter,
so do I purify the sinner, there is no doubt, / surely through the proper administration of medicines, and through bitter decoctions,
and through hot waters and torments, in the form of a physician, not otherwise. / Others enjoy other desired pleasures before his very eyes.
Though capable, [he laments,] 'What shall I do? I did not give excellent gifts.' / One should encompass this man in the form of severe disease.
Because the regular gift for oneself was not given by sinners, / O earthly god, with faith and according to their capacity,
so indeed will I burn those who arrive, by cruel means. / Now I will declare before you the occasion for occasional giving.
When a major festival arrives, and likewise when a sacred ford is reached, / on the anniversary of a father's death, and with effort in months such as Vaiśākha—
giving in these months and sacred times is known as occasional. / I will declare the occasion for motivated giving, which yields desired results.
Targeting a vow and the like, intended for the fruit of a desire— / that is properly called motivated giving, joined with all its parts.
Imbued with that intention, by the power of that giving, / a human being partakes of corresponding fruit through its grace.
I will declare giving for prosperity, which is commemorated in sacrifices and the like: / in birth ceremonies and such rites, in investitures of the sacred cord, and wedding rituals,
and diligently in the consecrations of temples, flagstaffs, and deities— / such gifts, O earthly god, are called prosperity-yielding.
It brings increase of offspring, enjoyment, fame, heaven, and happiness. / And now I will declare the final gift; listen, O best of the twice-born.
Knowing that desire has vanished, afflicted by old age, / one should diligently give gifts and have no expectation from anyone.
[Thinking,] 'When I am dead, my sons, wife, kinsmen, uterine brothers, / and my friends—how will these go on without me?'
Or [thinking,] 'Bereft of wealth, how shall I go on living once again?'— / thinking thus, he gives nothing at all.
Bound by hundreds of bonds of expectation through evil delusion resulting from fate, / the foolish-minded soul goes to death, and then his sons weep.
Afflicted somewhat by grief, their minds troubled by delusion, / they somehow prepare a very meager gift.
When that time is gone, when that great sorrow is passed, / they then forget about giving, or out of greed they do not give at all.
Knowing, 'This father is dead,' the bond of affection departs. / He who dies, O earthly god, bound by my nooses,
overcome by thirst and hunger, afflicted by many sorrows, / cooks in a terrible hell for a long time, there is no doubt.
Therefore, gifts should be given by oneself alone, without a doubt. / Whose sons, whose grandsons, whose wife, or whose wealth are they?
In saṃsāra, no one belongs to anyone; therefore, let one give for oneself / drink, food, betel, water, and gold,
garments, a cow, land, umbrellas, and various vessels, / fruits, and various gifts of land, according to one's capacity.
These should be given, O earthly god; no hesitation should be made here. / O brāhmaṇa, I will declare before you the characteristics of sacred fords.
These are auspicious fords: this Gaṅgā shines, the sacred Sarasvatī, / the Revā, Yamunā, Tāpī, and the Carmaṇvatī river,
the Sarayū, the excellent Veṇī, the Pūrṇā that destroys sin, / the Kāverī, the Kapilā, and another, the Viśalyā which saves all,
the celebrated Godāvarī, the Tuṅgabhadrā, and the Gaṇḍakī; / the river Bhīmarathī is known as always dispelling fear of sins,
the Devikā, and the Kṛṣṇagaṅgā, and others that are the best of rivers. / In auspicious times, these are sacred fords in many ways.
Whether in a village or in a forest, rivers are everywhere purifying; / in those very places rites such as bathing and giving should be performed.
When the name of that sacred ford is not known, O twice-born, / then one should utter: 'This is a great sacred ford of Viṣṇu.'
Viṣṇu is the deity of the sacred ford everywhere, without a doubt. / When a practitioner remembers the name 'Nārāyaṇa' at sacred fords,
the full fruit of that sacred ford arises through Viṣṇu's name alone; / for unknown sacred fords and deities, there is no doubt,
a human being should recite the names through the name of Viṣṇu alone. / All sacred accomplishments are holy; the ocean is indeed a sacred ford;
lakes such as Mānasa, cascades, small pools, and the like, / and even minor streams—all of them are sacred fords through the name of Hari.
Mountains are forms of sacred fords, as are a sacrifice and the ground of sacrifice, / and wherever learned brāhmaṇas reside, even for sport—
that very place is considered a very great sacred ford that removes all sin; / also a ancestral rite, ancestral ground, a temple, and an oblation area,
where the sound of the Vedas resounds properly, where auspicious stories of Viṣṇu are told, / one's own house endowed with merit, and a cow-pen is purifying as well.
Where there is an aśvattha tree in a forest, where a house is purifying, / such are sacred fords; and likewise a father and a mother.
Where food is cooked for the sake of dharma, where the teacher himself resides, / where a virtuous wife is present, there is a sacred ford, there is no doubt.
Where a learned son is engaged, constantly devoted to dharma, / there that sacred ford is established for his deliverance.

Sacred places such as these, as well as the royal dwelling,
and especially at these sacred places on the conjunction of festive days.
Without worshipping Hṛṣīkeśa, who grants all things to all embodied beings, / no one anywhere attains anything here—this is certain.

Offspring, wealth, wives, high mansions, horses, and elephants,
pleasures, heaven, and liberation are not far away through devotion to Hari.

Nārāyaṇa is the supreme deity, Janārdana whose nature is truth.
The Blessed Lord, the supreme master, produced himself in threefold form.

Joined with rajas and tamas, the pervasive Lord became predominantly rajas and sattva;
he produced Brahmā, seated upon a lotus, in the navel-lotus.

Associated with rajas and tamas, the pervasive Lord created Rudra.
Sattva, rajas, and tamas are thus declared to be this triad.

Through sattva a living being is liberated; sattva is of the nature of Nārāyaṇa.
Through rajas conjoined with sattva, one becomes prosperous and richly endowed with renown.

The Vedic declaration of dharma which one approaches and serves,
that is renowned as Rudra; it is declared to be distinguished for human beings.

Through it one becomes a king in the world, yet through rajas and tamas.
Whatever dharma is devoid of rajas and is purely an accumulation of tamas,

that brings misfortune to men in this world and the next.
He who is Viṣṇu is himself Brahmā; he who is Brahmā is himself Hara.

All three gods are worshipped constantly in this sacrifice among the gods.
O best of brahmins, whatever brahmin makes a distinction among these three,

that evil-doer, sinful at soul, will attain an undesirable fate.
Viṣṇu alone is the supreme Brahman; Viṣṇu alone is the world, O brahmin.

This month of Mādhava is dear to him above all ritual actions.
It is proclaimed as bestowing the fruits of great sacrifices such as the horse sacrifice,
exceeding the fruit of bathing at sacred places, asceticism, giving, recitation of mantras, and sacrifice.

Those who regularly bathe at dawn in a river when the sun is in Aries,
and who also perform the worship of brahmins in this [month], do not suffer my punishment.

Striking and striking the host of my servants before me, wiping and wiping away the writing of Citragupta,
bathing and bathing at a sacred place in the month of Mādhava, they rescue their ancestors here from sin.

This eliminates fear; therefore, this supreme secret should not be revealed.
It causes an expulsion from the realm of hell and brings about the destruction of my authority.

The Bhāgīrathī, the Narmadā, the Yamunā, the Sarasvatī,
the Viśokā, and the Vitastā are situated north of the Vindhya [mountains].

The Godāvarī, the Bhīmarathī, the Tuṅgabhadrā, the Devikā,
the Tāpī, and the Payoṣṇī are proclaimed to be south of the Vindhyas.

These twelve great rivers are continually entered by him
who according to rule bathes at dawn in a river during Vaiśākha.

All [rivers] flowing to the ocean are sacred, all best of mountains are sacred,
all sanctuaries are sacred, and all forest retreats are sacred.

They are plunged into, seen, bowed to, and extensively visited by him
who unfailingly performs bathing at half-sunrise during Vaiśākha.

O earthly deity, no one is able to recount his merit.
Even if there were thousands of thousands of mouths,

and the lifespan [allotted] by Brahmā were not brief, O best of brahmins,
even then [only] would the fruit of the month of Mādhava be capable of being told.

The month of Mādhava is like an all-consuming fire to the great hell; just as Mādhava [is],
[so it burns] the sin of killing a brahmin and the like, approaching forbidden women and the like,

sin committed intentionally or unintentionally, mortal sin,
minor sins, secret sins, and the supreme crime of causing mixture of castes,

dreadful offenses causing loss of caste, disqualification from ritual,
and the diverse impurities born of speech, mind, and body—

the month of Mādhava burns them away when observed according to rule.
For thousands of crores of eons and hundreds of crores of eons,
the prosperous man who worships Hari in the month of Mādhava shall dwell in the city of Viṣṇu.
